Predatory

/PRED-uh-tor-ee/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Predatory means living by hunting and killing other animals for food.

The dragonfly nymph is the pond's most predatory insect, taking tadpoles twice its own length.

Worked Example

A camera trap at a Kenyan waterhole records the same leopard on eleven nights. On six of them it stalks, kills, and eats an impala or a warthog; on the others it hunts without success and goes hungry. It never touches the carcasses the hyenas abandon nearby, and it eats no plant matter at all. The keeper's notes sum the animal up in a single word: predatory.

An animal that stalks and kills live prey on six nights out of eleven, refuses carrion, and eats no plants lives by hunting, which is what predatory means.

How Predatory Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

hunting

hunting: pursuing and killing prey

carnivorous

carnivorous: feeding on the flesh of animals

Antonyms

herbivorous

herbivorous: feeding on plants

scavenging

scavenging: feeding on animals that are already dead

How Strong Is It? — carnivorous → predatory → rapacious

carnivorous vs. predatory

carnivorous vs. predatory: Carnivorous says only that an animal eats meat, while predatory adds that it catches and kills that meat itself.

rapacious vs. predatory

rapacious vs. predatory: Rapacious is stronger and more judgemental than predatory, suggesting greed that runs well past need.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of predatory.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — pred-

Root — pred-: prey, plunder (Latin praeda)

Suffix — -atory

Suffix — -atory: having to do with; given to

Put it together

Put it together: Latin praeda meant booty or prey, whatever a hunter or an army carried off. Praedator was the one who carried it off, and English kept both the noun predator and the adjective predatory. The plain English word prey descends from the same praeda, and the formal noun depredation still names the plundering itself.

Use the root in a new word: depredation

Use the root in a new word: depredation: The depredations of an invading army are its plunderings, from the same Latin praeda ('prey, plunder') that stands behind predatory.
